one_liner: C HTTP/1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 web server and reverse proxy; 2016 charts show more req/s per core than nginx 1.9.
what_it_does: H2O is a standalone web server that serves static files, reverse-proxies, runs FastCGI and terminates TLS. You configure it in YAML (h2o.conf) and can script it with mruby (Rack-style handlers). It fills the same roles as nginx, but nginx.conf and nginx modules do not carry over. The same code builds as libh2o, a C library you embed in your own event loop (evloop or libuv) with an h2o_context_t per thread.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker thread (default: one per CPU) runs its own epoll/kqueue event loop (h2o_evloop). Requests are parsed with PicoHTTPParser, which has an SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI range-scan path, and short-lived objects come from per-thread memory pools and recycling allocators. The open-file cache is a khash + LRU table of file descriptors, with stat, ETag and Last-Modified strings, that is cleared at the end of every event-loop iteration: repeat hits in one iteration skip open/fstat, and replaced files are seen on the next iteration. For page-load time, H2O fully implements HTTP/2 dependency and weight prioritization and sends CSS/JS first for browsers that do not use dependency priorities. On high-RTT, small-cwnd links it also keeps unsent data small with TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT and TCP_INFO, so a higher-priority response can go out sooner. Newer optional paths include the picotls 'fusion' AES-GCM engine for QUIC, kTLS or MSG_ZEROCOPY TLS, and io_uring file reads.
when_to_use: Serving many small static files over HTTP/2 + TLS on one box: the vendor chart shows about 340K vs 77K req/s per core against nginx 1.9.10 for a 612-byte file
HTTP/2 front ends for browsers on mobile or long-distance links, where priority handling and the TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT latency tweak (Linux and macOS only) cut first-paint time
An HTTP/3/QUIC-capable origin or proxy on x86-64 Linux, using quicly/picotls with GSO and the AVX2/VAES fusion AES-GCM engine
C programs that need an embeddable HTTP/1-2-3 server library (libh2o) rather than a separate proxy process
Request logic in a small embedded scripting language (mruby Rack handlers) instead of writing C modules
when_not_to_use: You depend on the nginx ecosystem (third-party modules, Lua/njs, existing nginx.conf, ops tooling): none of it transfers, and you must rewrite the config in H2O's YAML

You need versioned, tagged releases: the project stopped cutting releases in April 2023 and treats every master commit as stable (the last tag is 'tag-no-more-releases'). You pin and track commits yourself

Security-sensitive edges with no capacity to patch fast: GitHub lists 14 advisories, including 5 in 2026 (4 high: HTTP/2 state amplification, a QPACK stack overflow on musl, QUIC assertion failures and a heap overrun), plus HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (2023) and MadeYouReset (2025)
Cold-storage file serving: file reads use pread/sendfile by default, which block the whole worker thread on a page-cache miss. Only file.io_uring (Linux, off by default) avoids that
Platforms other than Linux: CI runs only on Ubuntu 24.04. macOS and FreeBSD are covered by packages, and kTLS, io_uring and zerocopy TLS work only on Linux

integration.form: static lib (libh2o, or shared with BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON) plus a standalone server binary; built from source with CMake
integration.dependencies: Required: CMake, pkg-config, OpenSSL 1.0.2+ (LibreSSL and BoringSSL also build) and zlib. Optional: libuv 1.0+ (libh2o libuv binding), wslay (WebSocket), brotli, liburing, libaegis, and ruby + bison for mruby. picotls, quicly, picohttpparser, mruby, libyaml and neverbleed are vendored under deps/
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (CMake adds -std=c99) with GCC or Clang; CMake 2.8.12 or newer; the Release build defaults to -O2
integration.platforms: Linux (the only CI target), macOS and FreeBSD (packages; kqueue backend), SunOS handled in CMakeLists. The fusion AES-GCM engine needs x86-64 with AVX2/AES-NI/PCLMUL/VAES; other features are architecture-neutral C
integration.thread_safety: Not documented as a guarantee. The design is shared-nothing: one h2o_context_t and event loop per worker thread, with h2o_multithread queues for cross-thread messages. libh2o users must keep each context on its own thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it fills nginx's roles (static files, reverse proxy, FastCGI, TLS termination, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) but uses its own YAML config, and nginx modules or directives are not supported

gotchas: The default build has no -msse4.2, so PicoHTTPParser's SSE4.2 path (#ifdef __SSE4_2__) is compiled out unless you pass it in CMAKE_C_FLAGS (for example -march=native)

The open-file cache is emptied every event-loop iteration, and its capacity defaults to 2x http2-max-concurrent-requests-per-connection. It saves open(2) calls only within one iteration and is not a long-lived cache like nginx open_file_cache
tcp-reuseport is OFF by default, so all worker threads accept from one shared listening socket. Turn it on to spread accepts across threads
HTTP/3 is labelled experimental in the README, and most of the 2024-2026 advisories are in the QUIC/HTTP/3 and HTTP/2 code
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick H2O when you want a finished, config-driven nginx replacement for static files and reverse proxying with HTTP/2 prioritization and HTTP/3. Sogou Workflow, also catalogued against nginx, is a C++11 async task engine: you write server code on it, and its win is on small generated bodies. Lwan (catalogued as HTTP/1.1) and libevhtp suit embedding a lighter HTTP/1 server in your own program.
verified_claims_summary: Two 2015-2016 vendor charts, both from single-worker runs: a 612-byte static file with 250 clients (wrk for HTTP/1, h2load for HTTP/2) between two EC2 c3.8xlarge instances. Bar heights put nginx 1.9.10 vs H2O 1.7.0-beta4 at about 74K vs 108K (HTTP/1.1), 45K vs 79K (HTTP/1.1 TLS) and 77K vs 340K (HTTP/2 TLS) req/s per core. On an 8 Mbps/100 ms netem link, H2O 1.5.0 over HTTP/2 finished a test page 0.09-0.36 s sooner than nginx 1.9.5 and painted first sooner on Chrome 45 and Firefox 41, but not on Safari iOS 9.0.1 (2.01 s vs 1.85 s for nginx HTTP/1.1). No CPU model, compiler or build flags are given, and nginx ran with open_file_cache.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-10, 11.5k stars, MIT) and production-grade, but it ships from master with no numbered releases since 2019's v2.2.6/v2.3.0-beta2 and has a steady flow of HTTP/2 and QUIC CVEs, so plan to track master closely.
